A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Utility Learning work and its CATY-UL and TRACTOR-UL algorithms. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-F are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix F report original results from 15 participants, comparisons of utility functions, and numerical analyses of TRACTOR-UL.

after.justification: The original participant-based experiments remain, alongside a new analysis of non-Markovian behavior and simulations on randomly generated MDPs.

M1.justification: CATY-UL's classification rule changes from thresholding max_i C_i(U) to thresholding sum_i C_i(U), changing acceptance for multiple environments at a fixed threshold. The underlying risk-sensitive model, discretization, planning procedures, and TRACTOR-UL update remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates demonstrations from 15 participants in one fixed monetary MDP. v2 retains this coverage and adds randomly generated MDPs with noisy synthetic expert policies, including utility learning jointly across multiple environments (Appendix F.2.3). This introduces an important evaluation scenario absent from v1.

E2.justification: The comparison retains Ulinear, Usqrt, Usquare, and USG. v1's Table 1 becomes v2's Table 3 in Appendix F.3 with the same comparator membership. The added simulations evaluate TRACTOR-UL without introducing competing algorithms.

E3.justification: New simulations evaluate (S,A) configurations (20,5), (100,10), and (1000,20), plus N=5 and N=20 environments. They construct experts from an S-shaped utility with injected noise and use T=70, K=10000, L=10, and alpha=1. Section 6 also adds counting non-Markovian participant policies as a model-validation procedure. The retained experiments' settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic convergence analyses varying state/action counts and the number of environments, testing scaling implications of Theorem 5.2. It also analyzes the prevalence of non-Markovian behavior. The earlier learning-rate, initialization, and projection analyses are retained, including material moved into Appendix F.2.

E5.justification: Both versions document five seeded runs for the retained experiments and standard-deviation shading for the learning-rate curves. v2's explicit '5 seeds' caption repeats information already in v1's Appendix F.4. The new synthetic curves introduce no stated uncertainty-estimation procedure or run count.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports non-Markovian behavior in 10 of 15 participants and five synthetic convergence curves (Figures 27-29), supporting reported dependence on N and similar iteration behavior across larger S and A. These are additional results under new settings. The original utility-comparison values remain identical, including 28% mean incompatibility for Ulinear and 13% for Usqrt.

T1.justification: The relaxed feasible set changes from maximum to summed incompatibility. Theorem 5.1 and its proof acquire N-dependent discretization and N²/N⁴ sample factors, and the stated sample-size inequalities are corrected. v2 also explicitly assumes exact projection in Theorem 5.2, revises Proposition 3.2 to equality of optimal-policy sets under deterministic dynamics, and adds time/space complexity analysis in Appendix E.3. Several other propositions are merely relocated.

C1.justification: v2 strengthens the novelty framing around accommodating non-Markovian demonstrations, explicitly calling its model the first IRL model to do so in Section 6. The central contributions—separating reward and utility, characterizing partial identifiability, and providing two provably efficient algorithms—remain the same.

C2.justification: Appendix C.1 adds substantive arguments about the drawbacks of augmenting states with reward histories. Section 6 explains smaller learning rates with multiple environments through a smaller feasible utility set. v2 also distinguishes exact projection in the guarantee from approximate practical computation and softens the earlier overfitting explanation into a hypothesis requiring further analysis.

D1.justification: v2 supplies settings and an outline of synthetic expert generation in Appendix F.2.3, identifies the participants as lab members, and suggests quadratic-programming solvers for approximate projection. Existing participant questions, trajectory counts, hardware, and runtime disclosures are retained. Precise synthetic-generation and noise specifications remain absent.

R1.justification: The positioning is substantially reframed around non-Markovian behavior and analogies with inverse constrained RL, adding discussions of Malik et al. (2021), Kim et al. (2023), and other IRL work. Appendix A expands the Cheng et al. comparison and replaces broad criticisms of earlier risk-sensitive methods with more specific distinctions in behavioral models and environments.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, model motivation, applications discussion, and algorithm explanations are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a separate main section; Section 5 gains a dedicated problem-setting subsection; and the experimental appendix is reorganized. Acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout. The motivating MDP is redrawn as a numbered figure, the original two-panel experiment figure is split between the main text and appendix, and the utility-comparison table moves to Appendix F.3. Three new figures present synthetic simulations; many retained displays are resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful evidence on non-Markovian behavior and multiple-environment/scaling performance, improves the exposition, and makes the exact-projection assumption explicit. The gains are limited by incomplete synthetic-generation, noise, and uncertainty documentation. The new complexity analysis also has an apparent storage-accounting error: Appendix E.3 gives O(SAHN) for EXPLORE, although Algorithm 3 stores next-state probabilities requiring another factor S. Overall, the revision provides a modest improvement in support and clarity.
